name: Suno
tagline: Text prompt in, full song with vocals out, generated by a proprietary music model.

pricing.notes: AI-drafted from a site submission; price unverified.

verdictSummary: The app is a text box and a player. The thing you actually pay for is a music model that generates coherent multi-minute audio with intelligible sung vocals, and nobody is training that in an afternoon. Open weights exist for instrumental generation, MusicGen and Stable Audio and friends, and an agent can absolutely wrap them in a local web UI in one sitting. What you will not get is singing, lyric alignment, song structure that survives past thirty seconds, or the stem separation and extend features. The closest honest build is a local instrumental sketch generator, which is a different product wearing the same hat.
coreLoopDIY: A local web app where you type a prompt, pick a duration, and get an instrumental clip from an open music model saved to a library on disk.
requirements: A GPU with at least 12GB VRAM, or patience and a rented one
Python 3.11 plus PyTorch and enough disk for multi-GB model weights
Comfort with Hugging Face model downloads and CUDA driver misery
whatYouLose: Vocals: no singing, no lyrics, no voice at all from open instrumental models
Song structure: verse, chorus, bridge, a real ending instead of a fade at 30 seconds
Extend, remix, cover, and stem separation features
Audio quality that a stranger would mistake for a real recording
Instant generation without owning or renting a GPU
moatNotes: The training corpus is the unspoken asset here, and it is also the thing being litigated. Either way you cannot replicate it.
whyPeopleStillPay: Because generating a listenable three minute song with a singer in it is a research-lab capability, not an app feature. People pay for the model, and the credit meter is really a GPU meter. Even if the weights leaked tomorrow, most subscribers do not want to babysit an inference server to get a birthday song for their sister. The UI is the cheapest part of Suno and it is the only part you can clone.
notes: The player is a weekend; the singer is not. The moat is a music model plus whatever it was trained on, and neither is downloadable.
prompt:
Build a local instrumental music sketchpad called Riffbox. Single machine, no accounts, no cloud, no telemetry.

Stack, no substitutions:
- Python 3.11, FastAPI, Uvicorn
- audiocraft / MusicGen (facebook/musicgen-small by default, configurable to musicgen-medium)
- SQLite via sqlite3 stdlib for the clip library
- Frontend: one server-rendered Jinja2 page plus vanilla JS, no build step, no npm

What it does:
1. A page with a prompt textarea, a duration slider (5 to 30 seconds), a model dropdown (small/medium), and a Generate button.
2. POST /generate enqueues the job in an in-process single-worker asyncio queue so only one generation runs at a time. Return a job id immediately.
3. GET /jobs/{id} returns status: queued, running, done, or error. Frontend polls every 2 seconds and shows a spinner with elapsed time.
4. On success write a 32kHz WAV to ./clips/{uuid}.wav, then also encode an MP3 with ffmpeg if ffmpeg is on PATH. Insert a row: id, prompt, duration, model, created_at, wav_path, mp3_path.
5. The same page lists all clips newest first with an HTML5 audio player, the original prompt, a Regenerate button that refills the form, and a Delete button that removes the row and the files.
6. Model weights load lazily on first generation and stay cached in memory. Print a clear warning at startup if torch.cuda.is_available() is False, saying CPU generation will take minutes per clip.

Explicitly out of scope: vocals, lyrics, stem separation, track extension, multi-user auth, any hosted API.

Config in .env: MODEL_NAME, CLIPS_DIR, PORT, DEVICE (cuda/cpu/mps). Ship .env.example, never a real .env.

Deliver requirements.txt, a README with exact setup commands and honest first-run download sizes, and a make run target. Handle out-of-memory errors by catching them and storing a readable message on the job instead of crashing the server.
